```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)
library(NationalModelUng2009)
```

## What this workflow provides

This package predicts gross merchantable volume in cubic metres per hectare
(m3/ha) for the national models of Ung et al. (2009). Gross merchantable
volume is the volume of live trees larger than 9 cm in diameter at breast
height.

This workflow is for Carbon Budget Model (CBM) users and researchers who need
a volume-by-age curve for an area of Canada. The main output is a yield table:
one volume for each age, species, and climate. The table starts at age 0,
where volume is defined as 0.

## 1. Choose a species and climate

Choose a species by its common name, scientific name, or package code. This
example uses black spruce. The package can list the accepted names.

```{r species}
species <- "black spruce"
head(ung_species())
```

Supply climate values directly when you have them for the area. `dd0` means
degree-days above 0 degrees C: for each day, add the amount by which the mean
temperature is above 0 degrees C. `map` means mean annual precipitation in
millimetres.

```{r climate-values}
dd0 <- 2079
map <- 965
```

The two numbers above are the fitting-data averages for black spruce and are
used here only as reproducible example values. For a real area, replace them
with long-term climate values for that area. Use one `dd0` and one `map` at
every age; they describe the location, not a particular year.

`DD5` is degree-days above 5 degrees C, and `DD_0` is degree-days below
0 degrees C. Neither is the `dd0` input required here. If a location lookup
is useful, `ung_climate()` can obtain the values, but it needs an internet
connection and is not run in this vignette.

```{r climate-lookup, eval = FALSE}
site <- ung_climate(lon = -105.5, lat = 54.1, elev = 500)
site$dd0
site$map
```

## 2. Make the yield table

`ung_yield_table()` is the main function for a CBM input curve. Nat2 is the
default because it predicts average volume directly. Ages can include 0, and
the first row has volume 0.

```{r yield-long}
ages <- seq(0, 200, by = 20)
yield_long <- ung_yield_table(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  format = "long", warn = FALSE
)
head(yield_long)
```

The long format has one row per species, climate, and age. Its main columns
are `species`, `dd0`, `map`, `age`, and `volume`.

```{r age-zero}
yield_long[yield_long$age == 0, c("age", "volume")]
```

The wide format has one row per curve and one volume column per age. Columns
are named `vol_0`, `vol_20`, and so on.

```{r yield-wide}
yield_wide <- ung_yield_table(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  format = "wide", warn = FALSE
)
yield_wide
```

To make several curves, repeat the species and provide one climate pair per
curve. For example, `rep(species, 2)` can be paired with two `dd0` values and
two `map` values.

## 3. Quantify uncertainty

Uncertainty is a main part of using a volume curve. Ask for an interval while
making the yield table. The seed makes this simulation reproducible.

```{r yield-uncertainty}
yield_with_interval <- ung_yield_table(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  model = "Nat2", uncertainty = TRUE, n = 500, seed = 1,
  format = "long", warn = FALSE
)
yield_with_interval[
  yield_with_interval$age %in% c(0, 80, 200),
  c("age", "volume", "lower", "upper")
]
```

The `lower` and `upper` columns contain the central 90% interval by default.
It includes uncertainty in the climate values and uncertainty caused by
rounding the published parameters. The parameters were published to four
decimal places, and the unrounded values are not available.

This interval does **not** include the statistical uncertainty of the fitted
parameters (standard errors exist for Nat1 only, without the correlations
needed to combine them) or plot-to-plot variation. The default climate spread
describes differences among fitting plots. If the uncertainty of your own
climate source is known, pass it with `sd_dd0` and `sd_map`.

For a curve-shaped uncertainty plot, use `ung_uncertainty()` directly. Its
shaded band is the interval, and its line is the simulated median.

```{r uncertainty-plot}
fan <- ung_uncertainty(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  model = "Nat2", n = 500, seed = 1, warn = FALSE
)
plot(fan)
```

The `prop_outside` column reports the share of simulated climate values
outside the fitting-data range. A large share means that much of the interval
is extrapolation.

## 4. List all cautions with `ung_check()`

Run `ung_check()` on the long result. It reports each check, the number of
affected rows, and a plain-English explanation.

```{r checks}
checks <- ung_check(yield_long)
checks
```

With `warn = TRUE`, `ung_volume()` gives at most one warning per call. That
warning uses class `ung2009_warning` and is limited to problems the user can
act on: missing input, an age older than the fitting data, climate outside the
fitting data, or output beyond the fitting data. It does not issue separate
warnings for every row or every check.

The other cautions are still important for a curve. `ung_check()` lists young
ages, a projection horizon longer than the models' 10-year design horizon,
sensitivity to climate, and disagreement between Nat1 and Nat2. These checks
are not warnings from every `ung_volume()` call because they apply to many
ordinary yield curves.

If the inputs describe a typical stand rather than a particular area, omit
`dd0` and `map`. The package then uses the fitting-data average for each
species and reports the substituted values in the result. For CBM work,
supplying the climate for the area is usually clearer.

## 5. Compare Nat1 and Nat2

Nat2 is recommended when the required output is volume. Nat1 first predicts
dominant height and basal area `G`, then calculates volume from those
predictions. Nat2 predicts volume directly.

Use `ung_curve(..., model = "both")` for a short comparison. The default
Nat1 result is the published, uncorrected Nat1 model.

```{r compare-models}
comparison <- ung_curve(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  model = "both", warn = FALSE
)
comparison[comparison$age == 80, c("age", "V_Nat1", "V_Nat2")]
plot(comparison)
```

Uncorrected Nat1 is biased low. At age 80, across species at their average
climates, its median volume is about 20% below Nat2. This is because predicted
height and `G` carry more variation into Nat1 than its published volume
correction accounts for.

The optional `nat1_bias_correction = TRUE` applies a second-order Taylor-series
correction to Nat1 volume. It closes most of the gap with Nat2; it was added by
this package and is not part of the published model.

```{r corrected-models}
comparison_corrected <- ung_curve(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  model = "both", nat1_bias_correction = TRUE, warn = FALSE
)
comparison_corrected[
  comparison_corrected$age == 80,
  c("age", "V_Nat1", "V_Nat2")
]
```

Nat1 also returns `H_Nat1` for dominant height and `G_Nat1` for basal area
`G`. Plot `G` when that part of the Nat1 system is needed.

```{r basal-area}
nat1_curve <- ung_curve(
  species, age = ages, dd0 = dd0, map = map,
  model = "Nat1", warn = FALSE
)
plot(nat1_curve, what = "G")
```

## 6. Test climate sensitivity

`ung_sensitivity()` changes `dd0` and `map` up and down by 100 and reports the
largest percentage change in volume. It is a quick way to see whether the
curve depends strongly on the climate values.

```{r sensitivity}
sensitivity <- ung_sensitivity(
  species, age = 80, dd0 = dd0, map = map, model = "both"
)
sensitivity[, c("model", "volume", "dd0_change_pct",
                "map_change_pct", "max_change_pct")]
```

The `max_change_pct` value is the larger response to the two climate changes.
`ung_check()` uses 15% as a rule-of-thumb threshold for its climate-sensitivity
check. The threshold is not a claim from the Ung et al. (2009) paper.

## Limits of the models

The authors designed these models for increment predictions over intervals
shorter than 10 years. A yield curve over many decades is therefore a longer
projection than the intended use. Treat it as an illustration of the fitted
equations, not as a guaranteed forecast for a stand.

The models were fitted to plots measured once, where one species made up at
least 75% of the basal area. For a mixed stand, apply the model to each
species separately.

The climate terms describe how volume differs among locations. They do not
predict the effect of climate change, so do not use future climate projections
as model inputs.

## Reference

Ung, C.-H., Bernier, P.Y., Guo, X.J. and Lambert, M.-C. 2009. A simple growth
and yield model for assessing changes in standing volume across Canada's
forests. The Forestry Chronicle 85(1): 57–64. <https://doi.org/10.5558/tfc85057-1>
